title: Why can int4 and int8 rows take the same space?
answer: On a 64-bit build, Postgres gives every tuple a multiple of 8 bytes

checks.question: Would a row with two int4 columns take more page space than a row with one?
checks.answer: No. The first int4 ends at byte 28, and the second fills bytes 28 to 31, the padding one int4 leaves. Both tuples take 32 bytes, so both rows cost 36 and a page holds 226 of either.

checks.question: Would smallint (int2, 2 bytes) fit more rows on a page than int4?
checks.answer: No. Its tuple is 24 + 2 = 26 bytes, which the page rounds up to 32, the same as int4’s 28. Both rows cost 36 bytes and a page holds 226.

checks.question: With a 15-character text after the integer instead of an 11-character one, does int4 still fit more rows than int8?
checks.answer: No. After an int4 the tuple is 44 bytes, rounded up to 48; after an int8 it is 48, already a multiple of 8. Both rows cost 52 bytes, so the saving the 11-character text showed disappears.

steps.title: Do int4 rows fit more on a page than int8 rows?
steps.line: Predict: int4 saves 4 bytes a row. How many more rows fit in this page?
steps.caption: Postgres stores a table in pages of 8192 bytes, and every page starts with a 24-byte header, so an empty page has 8168 bytes free. A common way to save space is to declare an integer column int4 rather than int8 (bigint): 4 bytes a value instead of 8. Predict how many more int4 rows than int8 rows fit on one page.
steps.picture: An 8192-byte page drawn top to bottom, not to scale: a 24-byte header, then free space.; “Two ways to store the same rows”, 3 labelled values; 2 labels.

steps.title: One int4 row takes 36 bytes of the page
steps.line: Predict: int8 adds 4 bytes of data. How big is its tuple?
steps.caption: A row has two allocations: a 4-byte line pointer, which locates it on the page, and the row itself, called a tuple, at the other end: a 23-byte header padded to 24, then the int4, 28 bytes. On a 64-bit build the page gives each tuple a multiple of 8 bytes, here 32, so the row costs 36 bytes, of which 4 are the value.
steps.picture: An 8192-byte page drawn top to bottom, not to scale: a 24-byte header, then free space, then one 4-byte line pointer under the header and one 32-byte tuple at the very end of the page.; The int4 row’s 32-byte tuple in lines of 8 bytes, starting at offsets 0, 8, 16, 24: 23 header bytes, 1 padding byte, 4 data bytes, 4 padding bytes.; 4 labels.

steps.title: Answer: none. Both tuples are 32 bytes
steps.line: int8 fills the int4 tuple’s padding; a page holds 226 rows of either.
steps.caption: On a 64-bit build, Postgres gives every tuple a multiple of 8 bytes. The int4 tuple is 28 bytes rounded up to 32, so its last 4 bytes are padding, and int8’s 4 extra bytes take exactly their place. So an int4 row and an int8 row both cost 36 bytes, and a full page holds 226 of either: none more.

steps.title: A full page holds 226 int4 rows; 11.0% of it is data
steps.line: Tuple headers take 63.5% of the page, more than the data.
steps.caption: Inserts fill the page until the next row no longer fits: 226 rows. The pie splits the 8192 bytes, with each part’s bytes in brackets. The 226 tuple headers take 63.5%, more than the 11.0% that is the values: of each row’s 36 bytes, 4 are data. Each of these rows pays 23 header bytes for 4 bytes of value, so the integer’s width is a small part of the page whichever type is chosen.
steps.picture: Pie chart “One page of int4 rows”: 6 slices.

steps.title: Row 227 would need 32 bytes and a pointer; 32 are left
steps.line: Free space less a 4-byte pointer is 28 bytes, too few.
steps.caption: 226 rows of 36 bytes use 8136 of the 8168 free bytes, leaving 32; a new row needs both its pointer and its tuple. Reserving the 4-byte pointer leaves 28 bytes for a tuple that needs 32. The tuple’s own 28 bytes would fit; rounding them up to 32 is what keeps row 227 out.
steps.picture: Pie chart “One page of int4 rows”: 6 slices; “Why 226 rows”, 7 labelled values. Too small for another row: Free space: 32 (0.4%). New in this step: “Why 226 rows”, 7 labelled values.

steps.title: int4 and int8 fill 45 pages alike; with text after them, 55 and 64
steps.line: Both integer rows take 36 bytes; with text, 44 and 52.
steps.caption: Each line is a table of 10 000 rows, as measured on Postgres 18.6. int4 and int8 rows both take 36 bytes, so both tables take 45 pages. Put an 11-character text column after the integer and the padding is used up differently: the int8 table takes 64 pages to the int4 table’s 55. Whether a narrower type saves space depends on where the 8-byte boundaries fall.
steps.picture: “10 000 rows”, 4 labelled values. This scenario: int4: 36 bytes a row, 226 a page, 45 pages.

steps.caption: Postgres stores a table in pages of 8192 bytes, and every page starts with a 24-byte header, so an empty page has 8168 bytes free. A common way to save space is to declare an integer column int4 rather than int8 (bigint): 4 bytes a value instead of 8, here followed by an 11-character text column. Predict how many more int4 + text rows than int8 + text rows fit on one page.

steps.title: One int4 + text row takes 44 bytes of the page
steps.line: Predict: int8 + text adds 4 bytes of data. How big is its tuple?
steps.caption: A row has two allocations: a 4-byte line pointer, which locates it on the page, and the row itself, called a tuple, at the other end: a 23-byte header padded to 24, then the int4, then 11 characters after a 1-byte length, 40 bytes. steps.title: Answer: 28 more. The tuples are 40 and 48 bytes
steps.line: int4 + text: 185 rows a page; int8 + text: 157.
steps.caption: On a 64-bit build, Postgres gives every tuple a multiple of 8 bytes. Text needs no alignment, so after an int4 it starts at byte 28, in what would be padding, and the tuple ends at 40, a multiple of 8 already; after an int8 it starts at 32, and the tuple rounds up from 44 to 48. So a full page holds 185 int4 + text rows and 157 int8 + text rows: 28 more.
